claim: Color-vision deficiencies (CVDs) affect up to 8% of males and 0.5% of females.
source: To help maximize the impact of scientific journal articles, authors must ensure that article figures are accessible to people with color-vision deficiencies (CVDs), which affect up to 8% of males and 0.5% of females.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge about CVD prevalence rates.

claim: Most images published in biology- and medicine-oriented research articles between 2012 and 2022 included at least one color contrast that could be problematic for people with deuteranopia.
source: We evaluated images published in biology- and medicine-oriented research articles between 2012 and 2022. Most included at least one color contrast that could be problematic for people with deuteranopia ('deuteranopes'), the most common form of CVD.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' evaluation of images from research articles.

claim: Spatial distances and within-image labels frequently mitigated potential problems with color contrasts for deuteranopes.
source: However, spatial distances and within-image labels frequently mitigated potential problems.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' qualitative evaluation of images.

claim: 12.8% of images from eLife were determined to be difficult for deuteranopes to interpret.
source: Initially, we reviewed 4964 images from eLife, comparing each against a simulated version that approximated how it might appear to deuteranopes. We identified 636 (12.8%) images that we determined would be difficult for deuteranopes to interpret.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of 4964 images from eLife.

claim: The frequency of problematic images has decreased over time.
source: Our findings suggest that the frequency of this problem has decreased over time and that articles from cell-oriented disciplines were most often problematic.
evidence: This claim is based on longitudinal analysis of images from eLife articles.

claim: Articles from cell-oriented disciplines were most often problematic for deuteranopes.
source: Our findings suggest that the frequency of this problem has decreased over time and that articles from cell-oriented disciplines were most often problematic.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of images by subdiscipline.

claim: A convolutional neural network classified eLife hold-out test set images with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.75.
source: For a hold-out test set from eLife (n=879), a convolutional neural network classified the images with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.75.
evidence: This claim is based on machine learning model performance evaluation.

claim: The same convolutional neural network classified PubMed Central images with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.39.
source: The same network classified images from PubMed Central (n=1191) with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.39.
evidence: This claim is based on machine learning model performance evaluation on a different dataset.

claim: A Web application was created at https://bioapps.byu.edu/colorblind_image_tester where users can upload images, view simulated versions, and obtain predictions.
source: We created a Web application (https://bioapps.byu.edu/colorblind_image_tester); users can upload images, view simulated versions, and obtain predictions.
evidence: This claim describes a tool created by the authors.

claim: Most humans have trichromatic vision with three types of retinal photoreceptor cells sensitive to short, medium, or long wavelengths of light.
source: Most humans have trichromatic vision: they perceive blue, green, and red colors using three types of retinal photoreceptor cells that are sensitive to short, medium, or long wavelengths of light, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about human vision.

claim: Color-vision deficiency affects between 2% and 8% of males (depending on ancestry) and approximately 0.5% of females.
source: Color-vision deficiency (CVD) affects between 2% and 8% of males (depending on ancestry) and approximately 0.5% of females (Delpero et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delpero et al., 2005.

claim: Congenital CVD is commonly caused by mutations in the genes (or nearby promoter regions) that code for red or green cone photopigments.
source: Congenital CVD is commonly caused by mutations in the genes (or nearby promoter regions) that code for red or green cone photopigments; these genes are proximal to each other on the X chromosome (Nathans et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nathans et al., 1986.

claim: The genes that code for red or green cone photopigments are proximal to each other on the X chromosome.
source: Congenital CVD is commonly caused by mutations in the genes (or nearby promoter regions) that code for red or green cone photopigments; these genes are proximal to each other on the X chromosome (Nathans et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nathans et al., 1986.

claim: Deutan CVD affects approximately 6% of males of European descent.
source: CVD is divided into categories, the most common being deutan CVD, affecting approximately 6% of males of European descent, and protan CVD, affecting 2% of males of European descent (Delpero et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delpero et al., 2005.

claim: Protan CVD affects 2% of males of European descent.
source: CVD is divided into categories, the most common being deutan CVD, affecting approximately 6% of males of European descent, and protan CVD, affecting 2% of males of European descent (Delpero et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delpero et al., 2005.

claim: Both deutan and protan CVD are commonly known as red-green colorblindness.
source: Both categories are commonly known as red-green colorblindness.
evidence: This claim is based on established terminology in the field.

claim: Individuals with deuteranopia do not have corresponding green cones.
source: Individuals with deuteranopia ('deuteranopes') or protanopia do not have corresponding green or red cones, respectively (Simunovic, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simunovic, 2010.

claim: Individuals with protanopia do not have corresponding red cones.
source: Individuals with deuteranopia ('deuteranopes') or protanopia do not have corresponding green or red cones, respectively (Simunovic, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simunovic, 2010.

claim: Individuals with deuteranomaly do not have properly functioning green cones.
source: Individuals with deuteranomaly do not have properly functioning green cones, and those with protanomaly do not have properly functioning red cones.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CVD.

claim: Individuals with protanomaly do not have properly functioning red cones.
source: Individuals with deuteranomaly do not have properly functioning green cones, and those with protanomaly do not have properly functioning red cones.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CVD.

claim: People with deutan or protan CVD often see green and red as brown or beige colors.
source: People with any of these conditions often see green and red as brown or beige colors.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about color perception in CVD.

claim: 66,253 images were downloaded from research articles published in the eLife journal.
source: We downloaded images from research articles published in the eLife journal. Not counting duplicate versions of the same image, we obtained 66,253 images.
evidence: This claim describes the data collection process.

claim: 1,744 (2.6%) of the eLife images were grayscale.
source: Of these images, 1744 (2.6%) were grayscale (no color).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the downloaded images.

claim: 56,816 (85.6%) of the eLife images included at least one color pair for which the amount of contrast might be problematic to people with moderate-to-severe deuteranopia.
source: Of these images, 56,816 (85.6%) included at least one color pair for which the amount of contrast might be problematic to people with moderate-to-severe deuteranopia ('deuteranopes').
evidence: This claim is based on computational analysis of color contrasts in images.

claim: The mean, pixel-wise color distance between the original and simulated image exhibited a bimodal distribution according to Hartigans' Dip Test for Unimodality (p<0.001).
source: The mean, pixel-wise color distance between the original and simulated image exhibited a bimodal distribution, according to Hartigans' Dip Test for Unimodality (p<0.001; Hartigan and Hartigan, 1985).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of image metrics.

claim: 4,708 images (7.3%) had a mean pixel-wise color distance smaller than 0.01.
source: Specifically, 4708 images (7.3%) had a difference smaller than 0.01, while the median difference for the remaining images was 0.05 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of image metrics and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The median mean pixel-wise color distance for images with difference ≥0.01 was 0.05.
source: Specifically, 4708 images (7.3%) had a difference smaller than 0.01, while the median difference for the remaining images was 0.05 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of image metrics and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: 636 (12.8%) of the manually reviewed images were categorized as 'Definitely problematic'.
source: We concluded that 636 (12.8%) of the images were 'Definitely problematic', whereas 3865 of the images (77.9%) were 'Definitely okay'.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of 4964 images.

claim: 3,865 (77.9%) of the manually reviewed images were categorized as 'Definitely okay'.
source: We concluded that 636 (12.8%) of the images were 'Definitely problematic', whereas 3865 of the images (77.9%) were 'Definitely okay'.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of 4964 images.

claim: For images categorized as 'Definitely okay', shades of green and red or orange were visually detected in 2,348 (60.8%) images.
source: For the images that were 'Definitely okay', we visually detected shades of green and red or orange in 2348 (60.8%) images; however, in nearly all (99.3%) of these cases, we deemed that the contrasts between the shades were sufficient that a deuteranope could interpret the images.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of images categorized as 'Definitely okay'.

claim: In nearly all (99.3%) of the 'Definitely okay' images with green and red/orange shades, the contrasts between the shades were sufficient for deuteranope interpretation.
source: For the images that were 'Definitely okay', we visually detected shades of green and red or orange in 2348 (60.8%) images; however, in nearly all (99.3%) of these cases, we deemed that the contrasts between the shades were sufficient that a deuteranope could interpret the images.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review and judgment of image accessibility.

claim: Distance between colors mitigated potential problems in 54.2% of 'Definitely okay' images.
source: Furthermore, distance between the colors and/or labels within the images mitigated potential problems in 54.2% and 48.4% of cases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of factors that mitigated accessibility problems.

claim: Labels within images mitigated potential problems in 48.4% of 'Definitely okay' images.
source: Furthermore, distance between the colors and/or labels within the images mitigated potential problems in 54.2% and 48.4% of cases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of factors that mitigated accessibility problems.

claim: The percentage of 'Definitely problematic' articles declined steadily between 2012 and 2021, with a modest increase in 2022.
source: The percentage of 'Definitely problematic' articles declined steadily between 2012 and 2021, with a modest increase in 2022 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on longitudinal analysis of articles and is illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The decline in 'Definitely problematic' articles over time was statistically significant (p<0.001) using logistic regression.
source: Using a generalized linear model with a binomial family to perform logistic regression, we found this decline to be statistically significant (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of longitudinal trends.

claim: The number of 'Definitely problematic' articles differed significantly by subdiscipline (p<0.001) according to a χ² goodness-of-fit test.
source: A χ² goodness-of-fit test revealed that the number of 'Definitely problematic' articles differed significantly by subdiscipline (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of differences among subdisciplines.

claim: Cell Biology, Developmental Biology, and Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine had the highest percentages of problematic articles.
source: The subdisciplines with the highest percentages of problematic articles were Cell Biology, Developmental Biology, and Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis by subdiscipline and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Evolutionary Biology, Genetics and Genomics, and Computational and Systems Biology had the lowest percentages of problematic articles.
source: The subdisciplines with the lowest percentages of problematic articles were Evolutionary Biology, Genetics and Genomics, and Computational and Systems Biology.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis by subdiscipline.

claim: The best-performing single metric for predicting problematic images was number of color pairs that exhibited a high color-distance ratio (AUROC: 0.75; AUPRC: 0.34).
source: The best-performing metric was number of color pairs that exhibited a high color-distance ratio between the original and simulated images (AUROC: 0.75; AUPRC: 0.34).
evidence: This claim is based on cross-validation performance evaluation of individual metrics.

claim: Logistic Regression was the best-performing classification algorithm using the five metrics as inputs (AUROC: 0.82; AUPRC: 0.43) in cross-validation on the training set.
source: In cross-validation on the training set, the best-performing algorithm was Logistic Regression (AUROC: 0.82; AUPRC: 0.43; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on cross-validation performance evaluation of classification algorithms.

claim: All non-default CNN configurations performed better than Logistic Regression based on the image-quantification metrics.
source: All non-default options performed better than Logistic Regression based on the image-quantification metrics (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of CNN and Logistic Regression performance.

claim: The best-performing CNN approach used class weighting, early stopping, random flipping and rotation (threshold: 0.2), a dropout rate of 0.5, the ResNet pre-trained model for transfer learning, and model fine tuning.
source: The best-performing approach used class weighting; early stopping; random flipping and rotation (threshold: 0.2); a dropout rate of 0.5; the ResNet pre-trained model for transfer learning; and model fine tuning.
evidence: This claim describes the configuration of the best-performing CNN model.

claim: Logistic Regression classified the eLife hold-out test set images with an AUROC of 0.82 and AUPRC of 0.49.
source: Logistic Regression classified the images with an AUROC of 0.82 (AUPRC: 0.49; Figure 14; Figure 15; Figure 16).
evidence: This claim is based on evaluation of Logistic Regression on the hold-out test set and is illustrated in Figures 14-16.

claim: The CNN classified the eLife hold-out test set images with an AUROC of 0.89 and AUPRC of 0.77.
source: The CNN classified the images with an AUROC of 0.89 (AUPRC: 0.77; Figure 17; Figure 18; Figure 19).
evidence: This claim is based on evaluation of the CNN on the hold-out test set and is illustrated in Figures 17-19.

claim: For 92 hold-out images misclassified by the CNN model, reviewers determined that in 13 cases they had missed subtle patterns and it would be justified to change the labels.
source: For the 92 hold-out images that were misclassified by the CNN model, we compared them against our manual annotations and determined that in 13 cases, the reviewers had missed subtle patterns; we conclude that it would be justified to change these labels (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is based on re-evaluation of misclassified images.

claim: For 31 of the misclassified images, visual patterns were identified that might have confused the CNN, but the original labels were maintained as valid.
source: For 31 of the misclassified images, we visually identified patterns that might have confused the CNN; however, upon reevaluation, we maintain that the original labels were valid.
evidence: This claim is based on re-evaluation of misclassified images.

claim: For 48 misclassified images, no patterns were identified that seemed likely to have confused the CNN model.
source: For the remaining 48 misclassified images, we were unable to identify patterns that seemed likely to have confused the model.
evidence: This claim is based on re-evaluation of misclassified images.

claim: Of the non-grayscale PubMed Central images, 104 were labeled as 'Definitely problematic' and 1,087 as 'Definitely okay'.
source: Of the non-grayscale images, 104 were labeled as 'Definitely problematic' and 1087 as 'Definitely okay'.
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of PubMed Central images.

claim: The CNN model classified PubMed Central images with an AUROC of 0.78 and AUPRC of 0.39.
source: Again, the CNN model (AUROC: 0.78; AUPRC: 0.39; Figure 20; Figure 21; Figure 22) outperformed the Logistic Regression model (AUROC: 0.73; AUPRC: 0.16; Figure 23; Figure 24; Figure 25; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on evaluation of the CNN on PubMed Central images and is illustrated in Figures 20-22.

claim: The Logistic Regression model classified PubMed Central images with an AUROC of 0.73 and AUPRC of 0.16.
source: Again, the CNN model (AUROC: 0.78; AUPRC: 0.39; Figure 20; Figure 21; Figure 22) outperformed the Logistic Regression model (AUROC: 0.73; AUPRC: 0.16; Figure 23; Figure 24; Figure 25; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on evaluation of Logistic Regression on PubMed Central images and is illustrated in Figures 23-25.

claim: The percentage of 'Definitely problematic' figures in PubMed Central articles was 5.2%.
source: After manual review, we estimate that 12.8% of the figures in eLife would be challenging to interpret for scientists with moderate-to-severe deuteranopia. The percentage of 'Definitely problematic' figures in PubMed Central articles was considerably lower (5.2%).
evidence: This claim is based on manual review of PubMed Central images.

claim: 38.5% of the images from PubMed Central were grayscale.
source: One reason is that a much higher percentage (38.5%) of the images from PubMed Central were grayscale compared to those from eLife (4.4%).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of image types in PubMed Central.

claim: 4.4% of the images from eLife were grayscale.
source: One reason is that a much higher percentage (38.5%) of the images from PubMed Central were grayscale compared to those from eLife (4.4%).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of image types in eLife.

claim: Brettel et al. first simulated CVDs using the long, medium, and short (LMS) colorspace.
source: Brettel et al. first simulated CVDs using the long, medium, and short (LMS) colorspace (Brettel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brettel et al., 1997.

claim: Viénot et al. expanded on Brettel's work by applying a 3x3 transformation matrix to simulate images in the LMS space.
source: Viénot et al. expanded on this work by applying a 3x3 transformation matrix to simulate images in the same LMS space (Vinot et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vinot et al., 1999.

claim: Machado et al. created matrices to simulate CVDs based on the shift theory of cone cell sensitivity.
source: Machado et al. created matrices to simulate CVDs based on the shift theory of cone cell sensitivity (Machado et al., 2009; Stockman and Sharpe, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Machado et al., 2009 and Stockman and Sharpe, 2000.

claim: Frane found that 13.8% of color figures in psychology journals caused difficulty for at least one panelist with CVD.
source: Frane examined the prevalence of images in psychology journals that could be confusing to people with CVD (Frane, 2015). A group of panelists with CVD qualitatively evaluated 246 images and found that 13.8% of color figures caused difficulty for at least one panelist; this percentage is similar to our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frane, 2015.

claim: Angerbauer et al. found that on average, 60% of sampled published images were given a rating of 'accessible' across CVD types.
source: Angerbauer et al. recruited crowdworkers to analyze a sample of 1,710 published images and to identify issues with the use of color (Angerbauer et al., 2022). On average, 60% of the sampled images were given a rating of 'accessible' across CVD types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Angerbauer et al., 2022.

claim: Angerbauer et al. observed a slight increase in CVD accessibility for published figures from 2000 to 2019.
source: From 2000 to 2019, they observed a slight increase in CVD accessibility for published figures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Angerbauer et al., 2022 (implied from context).

claim: The analysis relied on deuteranopia simulations rather than the experiences of deuteranopes.
source: Our analysis has limitations. Firstly, it relied on deuteranopia simulations rather than the experiences of deuteranopes.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study methodology.

claim: The simulations used a single, relatively high severity threshold and do not represent the full spectrum of experiences that scientists with deuteranopia have.
source: Secondly, because we used a single, relatively high severity threshold, our simulations do not represent the full spectrum of experiences that scientists with deuteranopia have.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study methodology.

claim: Commonly used mathematical representations of color differences are unlikely to reflect human perceptions perfectly.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that commonly used mathematical representations of color differences are unlikely to reflect human perceptions perfectly (Bujack et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bujack et al., 2022.

claim: The CNN model's predictive performance dropped considerably when applied to the PubMed Central hold-out test set compared to the eLife hold-out test set.
source: Finally, our CNN model performed well at differentiating between 'Definitely okay' and 'Definitely problematic' images in the eLife hold-out test set; however, the model's predictive performance dropped considerably when applied to the PubMed Central hold-out test set.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of model performance across different test sets.

claim: The CNN model may have developed a bias toward patterns specific to image types that are over-represented in eLife.
source: Our model may have developed a bias toward patterns specific to image types that are over-represented in eLife, affecting its performance for other journals.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the drop in model performance.

claim: The PubMed Central Open Access Subset contains articles for thousands of journals, spanning diverse subdisciplines of biology and medicine.
source: The PubMed Central Open Access Subset contains articles for thousands of journals, spanning diverse subdisciplines of biology and medicine.
evidence: This claim describes the characteristics of the PubMed Central dataset.

claim: The diversity of PubMed Central is likely a factor behind the drop in CNN model performance.
source: It seems likely that this diversity is a factor behind the drop in performance.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of reduced model performance.

claim: Images were downloaded from eLife on June 1, 2022.
source: On June 1, 2022, we downloaded all available images from an Amazon Web Services storage bucket provided by journal staff.
evidence: This claim describes the data collection process.

claim: The eLife articles evaluated were published between 2012 and 2022.
source: These articles were published between the years 2012 and 2022.
evidence: This claim describes the temporal scope of the data.

claim: A list of articles from the PMC Open Access Subset was downloaded on March 21, 2024.
source: On March 21, 2024, we downloaded a list of articles from the PMC Open Access Subset, 2003.
evidence: This claim describes the data collection process.

claim: The colorspace package was used to facilitate deuteranopia simulations with a severity value of 0.8.
source: To facilitate these simulations, we used the colorspace package (Stauffer et al., 2015) and specified a 'severity' value of 0.8.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology for simulating deuteranopia.

claim: The severity threshold of 0.8 was chosen under the assumption that a mild severity level might not be stringent enough to identify a lack of contrast in the images.
source: We chose this threshold under the assumption that a mild severity level might not be stringent enough to identify a lack of contrast in the images.
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for choosing the severity threshold.

claim: The severity threshold of 0.8 reflects more moderate cases of deuteranomaly rather than complete deuteranopia.
source: However, because many people with deuteranomaly do not have complete deuteranopia, this threshold reflects more moderate cases.
evidence: This claim explains what the severity threshold represents.

claim: Neither of the reviewing authors (HPS and AFO) has been diagnosed with deuteranopia.
source: Neither of these authors has been diagnosed with deuteranopia.
evidence: This claim describes a characteristic of the reviewers.

claim: The reviewing authors did not play a role in defining the quantitative metrics to avoid confirmation bias.
source: To avoid confirmation bias, neither author played a role in defining the quantitative metrics described above.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological decision to reduce bias.

claim: The Web application was created using the Node.js framework.
source: We created a Web application using the Node.js framework (OpenJS Foundation, 2024).
evidence: This claim describes the technology used to create the Web application.

claim: The Web application implements the Machado et al., 2009 matrix for deuteranopia in Javascript with a severity value of 0.8.
source: For simulation, we implemented the Machado et al., 2009 matrix for deuteranopia in Javascript with a 'severity' value of 0.8, the same parameter used in training.
evidence: This claim describes the implementation of the simulation in the Web application.

claim: Tensorflow.js (version 4.0.0) was used to facilitate execution of the CNN within the Web application.
source: To facilitate execution of the CNN within the Web application, we used Tensorflow.js (version 4.0.0) (TensorFlow, 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the technology used in the Web application.
